back: Keep the source, ports, mode, and display unchanged. If replacing only the cable removes the symptom, the original cable path is implicated; flashing alone does not prove panel failure.

front: Why can a passive DVI-A-to-DVI-D cable fail even if its ends fit?
back: DVI-A is analog and DVI-D is digital. A passive cable does not translate signals. Use supported active conversion in the source-to-display direction, checking modes, connectors, and power.

front: How do you distinguish fuzzy projector text from geometric distortion?
back: Compare the projector menu/test pattern and source image. Check focus, placement, and native resolution for blur; check placement, aspect ratio, and documented keystone controls for sizing or shape distortion.

front: Does a faint old logo prove permanent burn-in?
back: No. Temporary image retention may fade; lasting wear is burn-in. Identify the panel/model, follow supported maintenance guidance, and escalate persistent marks without promising a software cure.

front: What is a safe response to persistent dark or bright pixel dots?
back: Use the manufacturer’s test, record positions/counts, and consult that model’s support policy. Do not press the panel or promise that pixel-fixing software repairs dead pixels.

front: What should you check before treating a dim or shutting-down projector as a failed lamp?
back: Identify lamp versus laser/LED technology; check settings, input, diagnostic indicators, ventilation and sleep timing using the model guide. Confirm the fault before authorized lamp service; follow its cooling and disconnection procedure.

front: HDMI video works, but there is no sound. What comes first?
back: Confirm speakers exist and check the selected audio output, mute and volume. HDMI can carry audio, but working video does not prove audio is routed to that display.

front: Confirmed burnt-out projector bulb: safe repair sequence?
back: Follow the model manual: shut down, disconnect power before opening, allow specified cooling, replace approved lamp module, then reset usage timer and verify operation.

front: Incorrect colors: how do you separate cable/settings from panel faults?
back: Compare the internal test, reset unintended color settings, and try a known-good cable. A defect in the internal test points toward the display.

front: Sizing issues: which controls match which symptoms?
back: Small projected frame: distance/zoom. Cropped edges: overscan/fit. Stretched picture: aspect ratio. Only UI/text too small: desktop scaling.

front: What proves a display repair is complete?
back: Retest the intended source, mode, image/audio, and original workload. For shutdown faults, run past the prior failure interval; document cause, fix, and prevention.

front: DoS vs DDoS: what does distributed describe?
back: Multiple attack sources. It does not specify reflection or amplification.
Reflection sends third-party replies toward a spoofed victim source. Amplification increases response traffic relative to the attacker’s request. Both can occur together.
No. C2 directs compromised systems and supports several malicious activities; seek evidence of the actual task.
The switch’s MAC learning/forwarding table. Unknown destinations may be flooded within the VLAN; behavior varies by platform.
Unwanted trunk negotiation (switch spoofing) and double tagging under susceptible native-VLAN conditions.
ARP poisoning installs false IP-to-MAC bindings using forged address-resolution information. MAC spoofing changes the address an interface presents.
Spoofing supplies a forged answer; cache poisoning stores false data for later use. The terms can overlap.
No. Validation provides origin authentication and integrity for signed DNS data with an appropriate trust chain.

front: Which DHCP options can redirect a client?
back: Router/default-gateway and DNS-server options. Compare them with approved configuration and identify the offering server.
A rogue AP is unauthorized. An evil twin impersonates a legitimate wireless network. It need not be wired into the victim LAN or use a specific channel.

front: Does a duplicate SSID prove an evil twin?
back: No. Legitimate APs share SSIDs; compare inventory, authentication settings, and other evidence.
A position between parties that enables relaying, observation, or manipulation. Credential theft alone does not establish that position.

front: Name the evidence source each social method abuses.
back: Phishing: deceptive communication. Dumpster diving: discarded information. Shoulder surfing: observed entry or display. Tailgating: another person’s physical access.

front: Can antimalware guarantee protection from phishing?
back: No. Credential phishing may involve no malware. Use layered messaging, identity, endpoint, and user-verification controls.
802.1X controls authenticated admission. Posture checks evaluate endpoint compliance; authentication alone does not prove up-to-date protection.

front: Why is MAC filtering weaker than device authentication?
back: A presented MAC address can be copied; it is not a cryptographic proof of identity.

front: What does an ACL direction mean?
back: Inbound or outbound relative to the interface where it is applied. Platform limits must be stated with the platform.

front: What makes segmentation enforce access policy?
back: An enforced boundary such as ACLs/firewalls with allowed and denied flows. VLAN creation alone does not restrict routed traffic.
One monitored decoy versus a network of decoys. Isolate and monitor them; they are detection aids, not replacements for prevention.

front: Why treat OT security changes differently?
back: Physical-process safety, availability, and device support constrain changes. Coordinate with process owners and test through an approved plan.

front: What is the first source for an unfamiliar laptop replacement?
back: The manufacturer’s service guide/parts list for the exact model and configuration; verify connector, part number, safety steps and required post-repair tests.

front: Does a battery-health percentage alone require replacement?
back: No. Compare vendor diagnostics, reported behavior, age and model guidance; replacement thresholds are product-specific.

front: When should you “calibrate” a lithium-ion battery gauge?
back: Only when the applicable device/vendor procedure calls for that model and symptom. A gauge recalibration cannot restore worn chemical capacity; do not make routine full discharges a general rule.

front: What should you do if a lithium-ion battery is swollen or leaking?
back: Stop use/charging when safe, do not press, bend, puncture or remove it, and follow the manufacturer’s safety/service guidance.

front: Why is charger wattage not enough to prove compatibility?
back: The device must also support the connector, voltage/current or USB-PD profile, cable capability, power direction, model requirements and (for some barrel adapters) identification method.

front: Which display uses the classic laptop “inverter” description?
back: A CCFL-backlit LCD, where an inverter drives the fluorescent backlight. LED-backlit LCDs use LED-driver circuitry; OLED has no separate backlight.
An LCD display with a dense LED backlight, often local dimming; the LCD layer still forms the image.

front: Can DDR4 SO-DIMM replace a DDR3 SO-DIMM because both are laptop RAM?
back: No. DDR generations use different electrical/keying requirements. Check the exact model support, module type, capacity and speed.

front: What can cause weak Wi-Fi after a laptop display repair?
back: A displaced, damaged, pinched or incorrectly routed Wi-Fi antenna lead is one possibility; check model routing and verify before replacing the radio card.

front: Before replacing a camera or microphone, what reversible checks help?
back: Check the hardware shutter/mute switch, OS privacy permission, selected device, application setting and built-in diagnostics.

front: Does a USB-C connector guarantee charging, video, or a particular data speed?
back: No. USB-C is a connector shape. The port, cable and endpoints must support the needed data/video/power feature and negotiated mode.

front: Can Bluetooth tethering share a phone’s internet connection?
back: Yes, when the phone, client OS/profile, carrier and settings support it. Pair and test the connection; Wi-Fi and USB tethering are other supported options on some devices.

front: What is NFC useful for when connecting accessories?
back: A very short-range tap can exchange a small record, tag data, or Bluetooth-pairing information. NFC is not a generic sustained high-throughput accessory link.

front: How does a port replicator differ from a docking station?
back: A port replicator repeats supported ports; a dock may add other controllers, displays or power. The product/model’s actual host and feature compatibility decides.

front: Does a webcam that fails in one meeting app prove camera hardware failure?
back: No. Check shutter, OS permission, selected input, app permission/settings and diagnostics before suspecting a part.
The sensing layer/system that converts pen or touch input into coordinates; it may be bonded into the display assembly rather than serviceable separately.
802.11ax; supported band depends on the AP/client.

front: What does Wi-Fi 6E add to Wi-Fi 6?
back: Use of 6 GHz by compatible 802.11ax devices where local rules permit it.
2.4 GHz and/or 5 GHz, depending on the device.
No; 802.11ac/Wi-Fi 5 is a 5 GHz generation. 6 GHz Wi-Fi 6E is based on 802.11ax.

front: Why is 2.4 GHz often a range choice, not a guaranteed speed choice?
back: It may propagate farther indoors, but has fewer practical channels and often more interference. Real performance depends on the environment and devices.

front: What changes as channel width grows?
back: The channel occupies more spectrum and may raise a compatible link’s PHY rate, but there may be fewer usable choices and more overlap/congestion.

front: Are channels 1, 6 and 11 a universal Wi-Fi plan?
back: No. They are a common 20 MHz U.S. 2.4 GHz plan. Country rules, device support, width and local interference matter.
Radar sharing on selected bands/channels: compatible APs detect radar and change or stop use as regulation requires.
It can improve signal quality toward a client and may improve performance; it does not guarantee range or throughput.

front: What does OFDMA add in Wi-Fi 6/7?
back: Resource-unit scheduling lets compatible clients share a channel more efficiently for some traffic patterns; it does not guarantee each client’s peak rate.
A compatible device can distinguish its own BSS from an overlapping BSS; spatial reuse may be possible for sufficiently weak neighboring signals. It does not erase interference.
A supported multi-link operation in which compatible AP and client devices can use multiple links under the selected configuration.

front: Why is a Wi-Fi PHY rate different from an internet speed test?
back: PHY rate is a link signaling rate; overhead, contention, retries, signal, client/AP capability, backhaul and ISP plan reduce actual application throughput.

front: What does WPA3-Personal use for authentication/key establishment?
back: SAE. Cipher selection/data protection is a separate part of the negotiated security suite.

front: Does “AES” uniquely tell you the Wi-Fi generation?
back: No. WPA2 and WPA3 modes can use AES-family ciphers. Identify authentication/key-management and cipher settings separately.

front: What can MAC filtering prove about the device that joined?
back: Only that the presented address matched a configured list; MAC addresses can be copied, so filtering is not strong device authentication.

front: Does hiding or changing the SSID encrypt Wi-Fi traffic?
back: No. Use an appropriate authenticated/encrypted security mode; SSID choice is a network name.

front: What does a 169.254.x.x IPv4 address suggest on a DHCP client?
back: Automatic configuration did not obtain a usable lease. Check association, link, DHCP server/scope and path; the address alone does not identify the exact cause.

front: A bulging, hot battery: what is the first action?
back: Stop using and charging the device, and replace the battery or device safely. Do not charge, puncture, or freeze it.

front: A cursor drifts on its own on a touch device. What is the fix?
back: Recalibrate the touch or pointer input.

front: A stylus stopped working but finger touch works. What do you try?
back: Replace the stylus battery or tip.

front: An app will not install on a phone. First check?
back: Free storage space, then check the OS version and account restrictions.

front: A laser printer shows residue from previous pages. Which parts?
back: The erasure lamp or the cleaning blade.

front: A laser printer prints a vertical black line on every page. Cause?
back: A groove or scratch on the EP drum.

front: An impact printer shows a blank horizontal line through text. Cause?
back: A printhead pin not firing; the printhead needs replacement.

front: A printer prints garbled characters. First fix?
back: Reinstall or update the correct print driver.

front: A print queue is frozen with many stuck jobs. What do you do?
back: Stop and restart the Print Spooler service in Services.

front: A printer feeds two or three sheets at once. Likely causes?
back: Damp paper or pickup tension that needs adjusting.

front: A projector shuts down and will not restart for about an hour. Likely cause?
back: Overheating, often from a clogged air filter.

front: A laptop's HDMI video works but there is no audio. First check?
back: The audio output setting and whether the volume is muted.
Account lockout after a set number of failed attempts.

front: Risk: a temporary worker keeps access after leaving. Control?
back: An account expiration date.

front: Risk: malware runs from USB drives when inserted. Control?
back: Disable AutoRun and AutoPlay.

front: Risk: booting from USB to bypass Windows. Control?
back: A BIOS/UEFI password and a locked boot order.

front: Lost company phone that will not be recovered. Action?
back: Remote wipe.

front: Tool that enforces screen lock and encryption on many phones?
back: Mobile device management (MDM) with configuration profiles.
BYOD: the employee owns the device. Corporate-owned: the company owns and fully manages it.
No. Degaussing works only on magnetic media such as hard drives and tapes.
A wipe overwrites data so it cannot be recovered; a quick format leaves the data recoverable.

front: Proof from a third-party destruction vendor?
back: A certificate of destruction or recycling.

front: What is a sandbox VM for?
back: An isolated, throwaway environment for testing software or investigating threats without touching the host or production network.
Run legacy software or an old OS, and run an app built for another OS (cross-platform).

front: How do three VMs reach the network with one physical NIC?
back: Each VM gets a virtual NIC, all connected to one virtual switch in the hypervisor, which uses the one physical NIC.

front: Does the host antivirus protect guest VMs?
back: No. Each guest OS needs its own security software and patches.
Virtual desktop infrastructure: desktop OS instances run as VMs on central servers and users connect to them remotely.
One app packaged with its libraries and dependencies, sharing the host OS kernel. Lighter and faster to deploy than a VM.

front: CPU feature Hyper-V needs, and where to turn it on?
back: Hardware virtualization (Intel VT-x or AMD-V) with SLAT and DEP, enabled in BIOS/UEFI. Hyper-V also needs Windows Pro or Enterprise, not Home. VT-c is a different, network-I/O feature.

front: Public vs private vs hybrid vs community cloud?
back: Public: open to any customer. Private: one organization. Hybrid: one organization using private plus public. Community: several organizations with shared needs.
IaaS: virtual servers and storage. PaaS: adds platform and dev tools. SaaS: a finished app.
Ingress is data into the cloud (usually free). Egress is data out of the cloud (often charged).
Elasticity: scale resources up and down with demand. Availability: the service is up when needed, such as 99.99 percent uptime.

front: Shared vs dedicated resources, and multitenancy?
back: Shared: a pooled provider resource split among customers. Dedicated: reserved for one customer. Multitenancy: several customers on the same hardware with separated data.
Keeps identical copies of files on several devices through a cloud service, such as iCloud Drive, Google Drive or OneDrive.
The software that creates and manages virtual machines.

front: Main drawback of a Type 2 hypervisor?
back: The guests compete with the host OS for CPU, RAM and disk.

front: Which hypervisor type for server virtualization?
back: Type 1 (bare metal), because it runs directly on the hardware.

front: Which hypervisor type for a developer testing on three OSs from a laptop?
back: Type 2, installed on top of the existing host OS.

front: Test and development use of a VM?
back: Run code on several OS versions without extra computers, and roll back with snapshots.
Running an application built for one OS on a computer that runs another.

front: RAM a host needs for a Windows 11 host (4 GB) and one 2 GB guest?
back: At least 6 GB: the host needs plus every running guest.
Each VM has a virtual disk file on the host, so the host needs free space for every guest.
A container shares the host OS kernel and carries only the app and dependencies. A VM has its own guest OS.
Pro and Enterprise. Home cannot run Hyper-V.

front: Who patches the guest OS in IaaS, PaaS and SaaS?
back: IaaS: the customer. PaaS and SaaS: the provider.

front: Which model for several universities sharing one research cloud?
back: Community cloud.

front: Which model keeps sensitive data private and uses public capacity for peaks?
back: Hybrid cloud.

front: Which cloud model is usually cheapest?
back: Public cloud: no hardware to buy and you pay for use.
Usage is measured and billed for what you use.

front: Which has less downtime: 99.9 or 99.999 percent uptime?
back: 99.999 percent (five nines): about 5 minutes a year, versus about 8.8 hours.
Extra servers added for a holiday sale and released afterward.

front: Does multitenancy mean customers can see each other's data?
back: No. Customers share hardware, but the provider keeps their data and apps separated.

front: What happens to unbuffered ECC RAM in a non-ECC motherboard?
back: It usually works as ordinary memory, with no error correction.

front: Which PC parts can make grinding or screeching noises?
back: Only moving parts: a mechanical hard drive or a fan, including the PSU fan.
Case parts: front-panel buttons and lights, front USB and audio, and fans.

front: Which M.2 modules fit an M-key slot?
back: M-key and B+M-key modules.

front: Does a SATA drive work on a SAS controller?
back: Yes. A SAS drive does not work on a SATA controller.

front: First step for a slow, nearly full drive?
back: Free up space by removing unneeded files and apps.

front: Where does shared video memory come from?
back: System RAM. 8 GB with 512 MB shared leaves 7.5 GB.

front: Which laptop component runs through the hinge into the lid?
back: The Wi-Fi antenna leads.
Clean the printheads, replace cartridges, calibrate, clear jams.
Replace the heat-sensitive paper, clean the heating element, remove debris.

front: Which protocol does scan to network folder use?
back: SMB. Scan to email uses SMTP.

front: Which appliance bundles firewall and IDS/IPS?
back: UTM (unified threat management).

back: NTP.

front: Fans spin, but there is no POST. Is the power supply good?
back: Not proven. A PSU can spin fans and still output wrong voltages. Test each output with a multimeter.
A failing motherboard (or power supply). Replace it; reseating parts will not fix it.

front: A RAID 5 array loses one drive. What now?
back: It keeps working. Replace the failed drive and rebuild; a second failure before the rebuild finishes loses the array.

front: "Operating system not found," but the drive shows in UEFI?
back: The drive is detected. Check the boot order and remove any USB media.
The link light goes up and down repeatedly: a faulty cable, connector or switch port.
Delay that varies under load. Prioritize voice traffic with QoS.

Client-to-site: one user's device to the company network. Site-to-site: two offices' firewalls link whole networks.

front: After installing a laser printer maintenance kit?
back: Reset the page counter so the next maintenance interval is tracked.

front: How do you clean up toner?

front: Which extension is associated with a Bash or shell script?
back: .sh

front: Compiled program vs. script: exam-level difference?
back: A compiled program is translated before execution; a script is interpreted by a shell, command line, browser, or external interpreter.

front: What does a for loop do?
back: Steps through a defined sequence or range and repeats the loop body.

front: What does Get-Item do in PowerShell?
back: Gets an item such as a directory entry, environment variable, or registry key.

back: TCP 22; encrypted remote console access.

front: Public AI and sensitive data: safest rule?
back: Do not enter sensitive or confidential data unless organizational policy explicitly approves the tool and use case.

front: Why use an ESD wrist strap?
back: To equalize electrical potential and reduce the chance of electrostatic discharge damaging components.

front: Where should a removed circuit board be stored?
back: In an antistatic bag or other approved ESD-safe packaging.

front: What is the first safety step before internal PC repair?
back: Disconnect power, then follow the device's service procedure.

front: What document gives chemical handling and cleanup information?
back: The MSDS / safety data documentation specified by the product and workplace.
UPS can provide temporary power during an outage; a surge suppressor protects against spikes.

front: Incident evidence: delete prohibited material or preserve it?
back: Preserve it and report through the proper channels.

Information that can identify an individual.

back: The acceptable use policy (AUP).

back: The organization needs valid rights for the number and type of installations being performed.

front: Why is a rollback plan part of change management?
back: So the organization can return to the prior known configuration if the change fails or cannot continue.

back: Ask open-ended questions and restate the issue to confirm understanding.

front: You will miss a promised service time. What should you do?
back: Contact the customer, explain the situation, and reset expectations.

back: Architecture placement and traffic paths can dominate cost even when service unit prices look low.

front: Cloud benefits under changing demand — name the key design constraint
back: Agility shortens the experiment/provisioning cycle; elasticity adjusts allocated capacity as demand changes. Scalability describes the ability to handle different load sizes, including planned growth. Managed services reduce undifferentiated work, but customers still design permissions, data protection, service configuration and recovery. Global infrastructure helps place workloads near users when data-governance requirements allow it.

front: Distinguish the six Well-Architected pillars — name the key design constraint
back: Operational excellence concerns operating, observing and improving workloads. Security concerns protecting information and systems; reliability concerns correct operation and recovery after disruption. A decision can affect several pillars: rightsizing can improve cost and sustainability, while redundant capacity may increase cost while improving reliability. Identify the primary business requirement rather than assuming every question is cost optimization.

front: Migration strategy, discovery and organizational readiness — name the key design constraint
back: CAF treats adoption as organizational transformation: business, people, governance, platform, security and operations perspectives require owners and an actionable readiness plan. Discover dependencies before migration. Application Migration Service supports server migration; DMS supports database movement/replication patterns; schema conversion may be needed for heterogeneous engines. A migration test includes data validation, cutover, rollback and business acceptance.

front: Economics, licensing and total cost — name the key design constraint
back: Compare total ownership: hardware refresh, facilities, power, cooling, staffing, resilience, software licenses and unused capacity. Usage-based cloud billing changes the cost model but does not guarantee savings. Rightsize from measured CPU, memory, I/O and business demand before making long commitments. Consider data transfer, idle storage, resilience and operational effort; economies of scale do not remove these line items.

front: Service-dependent responsibility boundaries — name the key design constraint
back: AWS operates physical facilities, hardware and foundational infrastructure. Customers choose access, data classification and application behavior. Shared controls such as patch management have different owners at different layers. Managed services do not transfer responsibility for granting least privilege or deciding whether regulated data may be stored in a chosen location. Verify the actual service model in the scenario.

front: Governance, encryption and audit evidence — name the key design constraint
back: Compliance evidence is contextual: Artifact supplies AWS reports/agreements, not an automatic certification of the customer workload. Verify the services, Regions, controls and regulatory requirements actually in use. At-rest encryption and TLS in transit protect different paths. KMS policies and IAM govern use of keys; encrypting a bucket does not by itself prevent an authorized principal from reading data.

front: Workforce access, root tasks and credentials — name the key design constraint
back: Prefer workforce federation through IAM Identity Center and an identity provider. IAM users are long-lived identities when required; groups organize user permissions, while roles are assumed to obtain temporary credentials. Separate authentication from authorization. Managed policies are reusable; inline policies attach to one identity. Least privilege requires actions, resources and conditions suited to the task. Store secrets appropriately rather than embedding them in code or images.

front: Preventive controls, findings and security resources — name the key design constraint
back: WAF filters supported application HTTP/S requests; Shield provides DDoS protection. Firewall Manager centrally manages supported security policies across accounts. GuardDuty detects threats; Inspector reports supported workload vulnerabilities; Macie discovers sensitive data in supported S3 content. Use official security documentation, Knowledge Center, the Security Blog and security/compliance resources to verify behavior. Marketplace offers third-party products; neither a listing nor a security-service subscription guarantees compliance.

front: Operate once, automate repeatedly — name the key design constraint
back: The console is useful for interactive exploration. CLI commands support scripts; SDKs integrate AWS APIs into application code. CloudFormation models infrastructure declaratively as templates/stacks, including dependencies and repeatable changes. Choose repeatability and change control for repeated environments. IaC still needs permissions, parameter validation, reviews and safe handling of state/data; a template is not proof that every deployment succeeded.

front: Availability scope and data residency — name the key design constraint
back: A Region contains multiple isolated AZs; an AZ contains one or more data centers. A subnet belongs to one AZ; a VPC is regional. Edge locations support selected edge/network services and are not replacement AZs. For residency, select permitted processing/storage locations; do not assume more Regions are always required or allowed. For global content delivery, distinguish edge caching from deploying a second application/database Region.

front: Compute families and scaling roles — name the key design constraint
back: General-purpose, compute-optimized, memory-optimized and storage-optimized instance families fit different bottlenecks. Measure CPU, memory, local I/O and networking rather than defaulting to the largest instance. Auto Scaling maintains/adjusts capacity; a load balancer distributes requests. Deployment across AZs and externalized session state are separate availability decisions.

front: Database models and migration responsibilities — name the key design constraint
back: RDS/Aurora fit relational workloads; DynamoDB provides key-value/document access patterns; ElastiCache supplies in-memory caching; Redshift is a data warehouse. These are workload models, not a ranking of universally better databases. DMS supports supported database migration/replication with cutover planning. Heterogeneous migrations can require schema conversion and application changes; moving rows does not prove all procedures, types and queries are compatible.

front: Network services and traffic paths — name the key design constraint
back: VPC routes select next hops; security groups and NACLs filter traffic at different scopes. Stateful security groups track return traffic; stateless NACL rules require the appropriate return path. Route 53 supplies DNS and routing policies. CloudFront supplies content delivery/caching; Global Accelerator improves paths to supported regional TCP/UDP endpoints. Match content distribution versus network acceleration requirements.

front: Storage classes, retrieval and recovery — name the key design constraint
back: S3 is object storage, EBS is persistent block storage in an AZ, instance store is ephemeral, and EFS/FSx provide file-system options. Select access model, sharing, persistence, latency and availability before price. Lifecycle can transition or expire eligible objects by date/age; versioning, replication and AWS Backup serve different recovery needs. A transition policy is not an immutable-retention control, and a replica is not proof of a tested restore.

front: AI/ML and analytics service selection — name the key design constraint
back: SageMaker AI supports building/training/deploying models; Lex builds conversational interfaces. A managed service does not eliminate data-quality, permissions, evaluation and governance decisions. Choose by the work: conversational intent, model training, ad hoc query, streaming processing, managed delivery, transformation or visualization. A multi-service pipeline may use several of these capabilities.

front: Recognize the service categories beyond core infrastructure — name the key design constraint
back: Integration: SQS queues work, SNS publishes to subscribers, EventBridge routes events, and Step Functions coordinates workflows. Select delivery and coordination behavior rather than matching the word event alone. Amplify supports frontend/mobile application development; IoT Core supports connecting/managing interactions with IoT devices. AWS Support is customer enablement. Verify current availability and the actual service capability before selecting a product merely by category.

front: Purchase commitments, capacity and transfer — name the key design constraint
back: On-Demand avoids a long-term commitment. Savings Plans commit an eligible hourly spend for a term; Reserved Instance discounts have scope/attribute rules. A regional RI discount does not itself reserve capacity in a selected AZ; capacity reservation is a separate requirement. Review RI flexibility and eligible consolidated-billing discount sharing within Organizations. Data transfer into/out of services, across AZs/Regions and to users has service-specific rules. Storage pricing includes requests, retrieval, minimum durations and transitions as well as stored GB.

front: Estimate, observe, allocate and alert — name the key design constraint
back: Pricing Calculator estimates a planned design from assumptions. Cost Explorer analyzes costs/usage and supports forecasts; detailed billing exports support more granular analysis. None of these validates a bad architecture assumption automatically. Organizations provides consolidated billing. Apply and activate eligible cost-allocation tag keys for billing analysis; merely attaching a tag does not guarantee its immediate appearance in reports. Account boundaries and allocation rules determine financial ownership.

front: Support choices and escalation resources — name the key design constraint
back: Current AWS documentation lists Basic Support and paid offerings including Business Support+, Enterprise Support and Unified Operations. Compare current technical-support scope, response targets and designated guidance rather than memorizing retired plan names or treating response targets as resolution guarantees. AWS Partners include software vendors and integrators; Marketplace distributes third-party products and purchasing entitlements. Professional Services and solutions architects address different assistance needs. Report suspected AWS-resource abuse through the appropriate Trust and Safety process, rather than sending it to an unrelated billing alert.

front: Evaluate a complete authorization request — name the key design constraint
back: Identify the principal (human, role or role session), action, resource, account boundary and conditions before evaluating policy. Federate workforce access where appropriate; use roles/STS for temporary workload credentials. For cross-account role use, the target role trust permits the source principal, the caller has sts:AssumeRole permission and the assumed role has required resource permissions. Control Tower and Organizations provide multi-account governance; choose the least privilege that matches the workload.

front: Secure the request path and application identity — name the key design constraint
back: Separate public entry points, private application tiers and data stores. Security groups permit required resource flows; NACLs evaluate ordered stateless subnet rules including return traffic. A private subnet name or missing public IPv4 is not proof of isolation for every address family. WAF filters supported HTTP/S attacks, Shield addresses DDoS, GuardDuty detects threats, Inspector assesses vulnerabilities and Cognito can provide application user identity. These controls solve separate problems; workload credentials belong in suitable role/secret mechanisms.

front: Keys, retention, recovery and sharing — name the key design constraint
back: KMS key policies, IAM permissions and encryption context/conditions determine key use; encrypting data does not neutralize an overly broad read permission. Plan key rotation/lifecycle and certificate renewal; ACM TLS certificates serve a different role from application secrets. Versioning preserves previous versions; replication needs both buckets versioned, permission/encryption setup and status validation. Existing objects need a backfill strategy. Backup, deletion recovery and Object Lock retention are distinct requirements; test recovery with the intended permissions.

front: Loose coupling with correct failure semantics — name the key design constraint
back: Use queues to absorb bursts and separate producer/worker scaling. SQS standard queues are at-least-once with best-effort ordering; processing must be idempotent. Visibility hides in-flight work temporarily, and successful processing must be acknowledged/deleted. Stateful sessions/files on one instance prevent easy horizontal replacement. Externalize appropriate state, choose container/serverless services based on runtime/operational constraints, and scale workers against backlog and processing time rather than an unrelated metric.

front: Failure domains, health and recovery evidence — name the key design constraint
back: Deploy independent serving capacity across AZs, configure load-balancer target health and ASG ELB health checks where application failures should cause replacement, and maintain enough surviving capacity. ALB can fail open when all targets are unhealthy; a health check is not a universal safety barrier. Choose DR from measured RTO/RPO and test data recovery, dependencies, credentials, quotas, routing and startup order. Backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby and active/active have relative cost/recovery tradeoffs, not universal minute guarantees. Workload metrics, logs and traces supply evidence of recovery.

front: Storage access, throughput and capacity — name the key design constraint
back: EBS provides persistent AZ-scoped block volumes; volume type and provisioned IOPS/throughput must match the instance and workload. A volume remaining after stop differs from DeleteOnTermination behavior. Instance store is scratch storage that can be lost on stop/termination or host loss. S3 handles objects with key-based access; multipart/parallel access, object size and request patterns affect performance. DataSync and hybrid gateways solve movement/interface needs rather than making every storage service interchangeable. Measure IOPS, throughput, latency and concurrency separately.

front: Choose and scale compute for the bottleneck — name the key design constraint
back: Match EC2 family/size to CPU, memory, storage, network and accelerator demand. Horizontal scaling needs a partitionable/stateless design; vertical scaling changes one node and retains its failure boundary. Benchmark before assuming the largest size is efficient. For Lambda, consider memory/CPU coupling, concurrency, execution limits and downstream connection pressure. ECS/EKS orchestrate containers; Fargate supplies supported serverless task compute. Batch/EMR target suitable batch/distributed processing. Placement/EFA choices have supported-instance and topology constraints.

front: Database access patterns, consistency and connections — name the key design constraint
back: Relational replicas offload suitable reads but may lag. RDS Proxy pools supported connections; reader endpoints distribute connections rather than guaranteeing equal query cost. Distinguish single-standby Multi-AZ, readable Multi-AZ clusters and Aurora read/failover roles. On-demand adapts capacity but retains warm-throughput/partition/table limits. DAX accelerates eventual cache hits, not strongly consistent reads. ElastiCache reduces repeated work where freshness requirements permit. Database-engine and migration choices require schema, transaction, query and compatibility analysis.

front: Network topology, transport and DNS behavior — name the key design constraint
back: Plan nonoverlapping address ranges, AZ subnets and route tables, including return paths and IPv4/IPv6 differences. Select gateway/interface endpoints, PrivateLink, peering or Transit Gateway from service exposure versus network-routing requirements. Route 53 weighted routing selects DNS responses probabilistically, with caching effects; latency routing uses AWS latency information, not simply map distance. Multivalue can return up to eight records and depends on health-check configuration, including an all-unhealthy fallback. DNS TTL limits how quickly clients observe failover.

front: End-to-end ingestion and transformation — name the key design constraint
back: Kinesis Data Streams supports streaming records consumed by applications; ordering is scoped to shard/partition-key sequencing, with producer retry and consumer checkpoint behavior to design. Firehose supplies managed buffered delivery and optional transformations to supported destinations. DataSync, Storage Gateway and supported transfer services address different movement and interface needs. Secure ingestion endpoints, roles, encryption, data-lake access and catalog governance. Design throughput, buffering, latency, replay and malformed-record handling together.

front: Price the complete storage lifecycle — name the key design constraint
back: Compare object/file/block access requirements before cost. Include stored bytes, provisioned performance, requests, transitions, retrieval, minimum-duration/object-size rules, replicas and transfers. The cheapest GB price may violate retrieval or durability requirements. Size persistent storage and backup retention from recovery/compliance needs. Delete only genuinely unused volumes/snapshots under policy; snapshot dependencies mean billed savings may differ from visible snapshot count. Compare DataSync/transfer/gateway options against scale, bandwidth and change rate.

front: Commit the baseline and scale the variable work — name the key design constraint
back: Right-size and measure before choosing commitments. Use eligible Savings Plans/Reserved discounts for a stable baseline; On-Demand for flexibility; Spot for interruption-tolerant work after accounting for capacity/restart behavior. A discount is not a capacity guarantee. Compute topology also determines load-balancing, network and resilience costs. Select ALB/NLB/GWLB and horizontal/vertical/suspend/hibernate choices from protocol, state and availability requirements. Outposts/hybrid choices add operational and placement considerations.

front: Database cost without losing correctness — name the key design constraint
back: Choose engine/model from transactions, access patterns, schema, scale and compatibility; compare relational, key-value/document, time-series and analytical workloads deliberately. A low instance rate is not a reason to select an incompatible data model. Backups, cross-Region copies, retention and migrations all cost money but meet different requirements. Heterogeneous migration needs schema/application validation. Estimate the cost of read scaling, data retention and recovery before eliminating safeguards for savings.

front: Network cost follows the traffic path — name the key design constraint
back: Identify bytes and paths: same-AZ, cross-AZ, cross-Region, service endpoint, NAT, dedicated link and internet delivery. Data-transfer pricing is service-specific; do not assume all same-Region traffic is free or all cross-AZ paths charge identically. Compare Direct Connect, VPN and internet designs using bandwidth, encryption, redundancy and business targets. CloudFront may reduce repeated origin work/transfer, but include CDN/request/invalidations and cache hit behavior. Do not minimize transfer by removing required failure isolation.

front: Application, OS and driver roles — explain the decision
back: An application performs the user-facing task; the OS supplies shared services. Drivers connect the OS to hardware; a filesystem organizes stored data.

front: ChromeOS can work offline — explain the decision
back: ChromeOS supports offline-capable applications and prepared local data. Offline availability depends on the app and file configuration; Linux has roles beyond desktops.

front: Source code and compilation — explain the decision
back: Source code is input to compilation in this workflow. Calling source code precompiled machine instructions confuses the input with the output.

front: Mobile operating systems — explain the decision
back: Android is a mobile operating system in the smartphone scenario. An OS category does not imply that every application or feature requires cloud access.

front: Preview versus production releases — explain the decision
back: Windows Insider distributes preview builds for evaluation. Preview channels and eligibility change; use current guidance and keep a recovery plan instead of old Windows servicing names.

front: Prepare an image before capture — explain the decision
back: Sysprep /generalize prepares a reference installation by removing machine-specific information. A WIM is an image format; capture and deployment are separate operations. Use supported imaging procedures.

front: Boot configuration data — explain the decision
back: BCD holds Windows boot configuration used by the boot manager. UEFI and legacy boot components differ; hibernation resume is not the same as a normal OS boot.

front: Static IP configuration paths — explain the decision
back: Windows network Settings can configure manual IP assignment for an adapter. Adapter properties reached through Control Panel can also configure IP; a question must constrain the path if only one answer is intended.

front: Fragmentation is still possible — explain the decision
back: ext4 uses allocation strategies to improve data locality and reduce fragmentation. These mechanisms are not a guarantee of automatic, continuous defragmentation.

front: Update macOS through Software Update — explain the decision
back: Current macOS updates are offered through Software Update in System Settings. App Store app updates are a different task; older macOS versions may use different paths.

front: Finder manages files — explain the decision
back: Finder is the standard macOS file-browsing interface. Browsing a file is different from installing an OS update or managing firmware.

front: Search names versus contents — explain the decision
back: grep -r searches matching text through files recursively. find traverses directories by default; -name matches entry names rather than searching each file’s contents.
Repeated candidate-password attempts are evidence of password guessing. The log does not by itself prove successful access. Investigate outcomes and apply approved authentication protections.

front: Biometrics and authentication factors — explain the decision
back: A fingerprint is a biometric characteristic. A PIN and password are both knowledge factors; a smart card/token is possession, not a biological characteristic.
A rootkit is associated with concealed malicious presence or control. A symptom is a clue, not proof; follow the incident workflow and use trusted inspection/recovery methods.

front: Physical security boundaries — explain the decision
back: A fence creates a physical perimeter control. Physical controls complement authentication and monitoring; a fence alone does not grant or verify digital access.
A metal detector detects metal under its operating conditions. It is not a universal weapon detector or a substitute for identity checks.

front: Sync is not independent backup — explain the decision
back: Synchronization coordinates selected data and may propagate deletion. Recoverability depends on retention, versioning and backup configuration, not merely having two synced devices.

front: Firewall rules and tamper protection — explain the decision
back: Advanced Security manages scoped firewall rules. Defender Tamper Protection restricts unauthorized security-setting changes; it is not the tool for authoring firewall rules.

Hardening combines maintained software with restricted access and appropriate authentication. Renaming an account alone does not prevent compromise; disabling protective controls weakens the baseline.

front: File encryption versus volume encryption — explain the decision
back: EFS provides file-level encryption on supported Windows/NTFS configurations. Do not rule out BitLocker solely because a TPM is absent: supported non-TPM configurations exist. Plan recovery of encryption credentials.

front: Verify folder-backup configuration — explain the decision
back: OneDrive folder backup requires the relevant client, account and folder configuration. A Microsoft account alone is not evidence that every file or folder is protected.

front: Built-in GPU performance monitoring — explain the decision
back: Task Manager can display GPU data with supported hardware and drivers. Third-party tools may add detail, but they are not always required. GPU support depends on the driver model.

front: End malware removal with education — explain the decision
back: End-user education helps prevent recurrence after the required remediation and recovery steps. Education is not a substitute for containment, removal, validation or the organization’s incident procedure.

front: Match Wi-Fi changes to evidence — explain the decision
back: An alternative supported band may reduce the measured 2.4 GHz interference. Range, obstructions and coverage still matter; 5 GHz is not a universal cure for disconnections.

front: USB controller-resource troubleshooting — explain the decision
back: USB devices can share controller resources even across different physical ports. Check power, bandwidth, controller topology and supported drivers; port generation/color alone does not establish the cause.

front: Virtual-machine clock synchronization — explain the decision
back: Virtual timekeeping and pause/resume behavior can cause clock drift. The correct time source depends on the configuration; domain members commonly use the domain hierarchy.

front: Manage a Windows service — explain the decision
back: The Services management console controls supported service operations. Review dependencies and the failure cause; changing startup settings is different from restarting a running service.

front: Battery thermal hazards — explain the decision
back: A damaged or overheated lithium-ion battery can present a serious thermal hazard. Follow manufacturer and workplace handling/escalation guidance; do not puncture, charge or improvise a repair.

front: Shutdown evidence versus cause — explain the decision
back: Unexpected-shutdown logs are evidence to correlate with other symptoms and records. A shutdown event does not independently identify the root cause.

front: RDP transport and default port — explain the decision
back: Direct RDP commonly uses TCP and UDP port 3389. Gateways and configured ports can change the path; do not assume TCP is its only possible transport.
REM records a batch-file comment. Comment syntax depends on the interpreter; PowerShell/Bash and JavaScript examples do not become cmd.exe comments.

front: Launch the RDP client — explain the decision
back: mstsc launches the Windows Remote Desktop Connection client. Launching a client does not establish authorization, reachability or permission to control the target.
A host-to-site VPN connects an individual remote client to the organization’s network. A VPN does not remove endpoint, authentication or application-authorization requirements.
Videoconferencing is the relevant collaboration capability. Platforms such as Teams/Zoom may also support chat, sharing and other features; one label does not exclude the others.

front: Verify AI-generated guidance — explain the decision
back: AI-generated technical guidance needs independent validation and policy review. Confidence and fluent language do not establish accuracy or permission; protect sensitive data.

front: Approved ESD controls — explain the decision
back: Approved ESD equipment and handling procedures reduce damaging potential differences. Hair restraint can address other hazards, but it does not replace ESD controls. Follow electrical-safety and equipment guidance.

front: Use the correct driver bit — explain the decision
back: Use the matching driver type and size to avoid damaging the fastener or equipment. Torx has a familiar six-lobed form; security variants can require a corresponding special bit.

front: Trial licensing and open source — explain the decision
back: Shareware commonly offers trial or limited use before purchase. Open-source software can be used commercially under its license; price and licensing rights are separate questions.

front: ESD strap resistance — explain the decision
back: Approved wrist straps commonly include a series safety resistor, often around one megaohm. Use the manufacturer-approved equipment and bonding procedure; this is not a universal instruction for every grounding system.

front: Choose PPE from the hazard — explain the decision
back: PPE and cleaning methods should match the actual hazard and approved procedure. A filtration mask can be appropriate for airborne particles, but it is not a universal answer for every task.

front: Microwave interference scope — explain the decision
back: Microwave-related interference can affect 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. Validate timing, signal and band conditions; this is not a claim that every wireless failure or band has the same cause.

front: Respect access authorization — explain the decision
back: Visible credentials do not grant permission to use another person’s account. The approved contact method may be a call, ticket or other channel; texting is not universally required.

front: Report accidental damage — explain the decision
back: Honest communication and documented escalation preserve trust and support safe resolution. Do not conceal damage or continue with a component known to be unsafe or faulty.

front: Communicate a changed estimate — explain the decision
back: Communicate delays and revised expectations proactively. An estimate is not permission to hide risk or mark unfinished work resolved.

front: Ticket intake depends on the workflow — explain the decision
back: The correct intake channel follows the organization’s configured and accessible workflow. Email, portals, staff entry and automated alerts have different uses; no one method is universally easiest.

front: Sandbox, rollout and backout — explain the decision
back: Sandbox testing isolates evaluation; a backout plan explains how to reverse a failed change. Blackout and backout are different terms. Approval, verification and recovery planning remain part of change control.

front: Rename and join an AD domain — explain the decision
back: System Properties provides computer-name/domain membership controls. Successful domain join also requires the correct edition, network/DNS reachability and authorized credentials.

front: Task Manager user sessions — explain the decision
back: Task Manager’s Users view shows signed-in users and their associated activity. The Performance tab provides resource graphs; it answers a different question.

front: RAID 5 is supplemental Core 1 storage — explain the decision
back: Conventional RAID 5 uses distributed parity and tolerates one member failure. This is supplemental Core 1 storage context. Degraded/rebuild availability depends on the controller and workload; RAID is not backup.

front: Which file stores hashed Linux passwords and is restricted to root?
back: /etc/shadow
Maps names to IP addresses locally; checked before DNS.
Owner rw, group r, others r (6 = rw, 4 = r).
sudo runs one command with elevated rights; su switches the session to root.

front: Why disable UPnP on a router?
back: It lets internal apps open firewall ports automatically, which is a security risk.

front: What is a DMZ on a SOHO network?
back: A screened subnet for internet-facing services that cannot reach the private LAN.

front: Why verify a browser installer with a hash?
back: Matching the developer's SHA-256 hash confirms the file is authentic.
Sideloading installs apps from unofficial sources; rooting and jailbreaking disable OS protections.
Malware disguised as legitimate software that does not copy itself and relies on the user running it.
It hides deep in the OS, often at kernel level, and can evade normal antivirus scans.
Malware that runs in memory with built-in tools such as PowerShell and leaves little on disk.
Vishing is voice phishing by phone call; smishing is phishing by SMS text message.
A fake Wi-Fi access point set up to copy a legitimate network name.
An attack that exploits a vulnerability before a patch exists.

front: Why disable System Restore during malware removal?
back: Malware can hide in restore points and return after removal; re-enable it afterward with a clean restore point.

front: What does EDR add beyond antivirus?
back: Behavior monitoring on each endpoint, such as a process trying to access files it should not.

front: What is the difference between a VPN and Direct Connect?
back: A VPN is an encrypted tunnel over the public internet; Direct Connect is a private dedicated link to the cloud.
Hardware network appliances, replaced by software functions running on standard servers.

front: Why do 2.4 GHz access points use channels 1, 6 and 11?
back: They are the non-overlapping channels, so neighboring access points do not interfere.
PSK uses one shared password; 802.1X authenticates each user against a RADIUS server.
The main distribution frame: the central wiring closet connected to the outside world.
A UPS is battery backup; a PDU distributes power inside the rack.
SSH encrypts on port 22; Telnet sends plain text on port 23.
Inbound uses the production network; out-of-band uses a separate path that works during outages.

front: Latency versus jitter versus packet loss?
back: Latency is delay, jitter is uneven delay, packet loss means the data never arrives.
Bandwidth is the theoretical maximum; throughput is what actually moves through the link.

front: Which file system is native to newer Windows and supports compression, encryption, and permissions?
back: NTFS

front: Which cross-platform file system stores files larger than 4 GB on USB drives and memory cards?
back: exFAT

front: Which file system is the primary file system on newer Macs, optimized for SSDs with snapshots and cloning?
back: APFS

front: Which Windows Server file system focuses on integrity checking and does not support compression or encryption?
back: ReFS

front: Which OS category runs on resource-constrained devices with real-time features, often based on Linux?
back: Embedded OS

front: Why is running an OS past its end of life a security risk?
back: The vendor stops providing patches, so known vulnerabilities stay open.

front: Which command lists the files and subfolders in the current folder?
back: dir

front: Which copy command mirrors a folder and can resume interrupted transfers?
back: robocopy (/MIR and /Z)

front: Which two commands release and request a new DHCP lease?
back: ipconfig /release, then ipconfig /renew

front: Which command clears the local DNS resolver cache?
back: ipconfig /flushdns

front: Which command tests reachability and round-trip time?
back: ping

front: Which command shows each hop and per-hop latency and packet loss?

front: Which command scans and repairs protected system files?

front: Which command applies Group Policy changes immediately?

front: Which Run command opens Control Panel?

front: Which power state saves the session to disk and powers off?

front: Which Ease of Access tool reads text aloud?

front: Which applet manages Outlook accounts, data files and profiles?
back: Mail

front: Which command-line tool views and changes power settings?

front: Which Windows Settings category manages Bluetooth, printers and peripherals?

front: Which network model has no central server and each computer manages its own accounts?
back: Workgroup

front: Which network model uses domain controllers for central management?
back: Domain

front: What address range does Windows assign when DHCP is unreachable?
Which IPv4 setting holds the router that reaches other networks?

front: Which macOS file type mounts as a virtual drive when opened?

front: Which macOS installer type runs a step-by-step wizard for drivers and system software?

front: Which folder stores applications for all users?
back: /Applications

front: Which folder holds a home directory for each user account?

front: Which protected folder holds the core operating system files?

front: Which hidden folder stores a user's preferences and caches?

front: Which processor type runs only a 32-bit operating system?
back: 32-bit processor

front: Which folder holds 32-bit applications on a 64-bit Windows system?

front: Which distribution method mounts a complete disk image as a virtual drive?

front: Which method deploys one preconfigured system image to many machines?
back: Image deployment

front: Which concept keeps one user account consistent across cloud services?
back: Identity synchronization

front: If a cloud app's features are disabled after sign-in, what should you check first?
back: Whether the proper license is assigned

front: Where is the real-time protection toggle in Windows Security?
back: Virus and threat protection, then Manage settings

front: Which firewall profile is most restrictive, for public Wi-Fi?
back: Public network profile
